title: The Covenant Lawsuit (rib)
aka: the LORD's case against his people
lead: A pattern in the prophets in which the LORD, like a plaintiff, brings a case against his own people before witnesses such as heaven and earth or the mountains, lists what he has done for them, states the charge and announces the sentence. The Hebrew word is riv ('case, dispute').

sections.b: The plainest examples are Deuteronomy 32, Isaiah 1:2-20, Hosea 4:1-3, Jeremiah 2:4-13 and Micah 6:1-8. In each, a call to hear is followed by the charge, a recital of the LORD's past kindness and the demand for an answer. In 1959 Herbert Huffmon proposed that the prophets imitated the legal procedure of a king against a vassal who has broken a treaty; Wright applied it to Deuteronomy 32. Others, such as Michael de Roche (1983), argue that riv is a wide word for any dispute and that no fixed genre has been shown.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2; Hosea 4:1; Hosea 12:2; Jeremiah 2:9; Micah 6:1; Micah 6:2

sections.b: Ancient treaties called on gods and on natural features (mountains, rivers, the sea) as witnesses. In Israel's use, heaven and earth (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 32:1; Isaiah 1:2) or the mountains and hills (Micah 6:1-2) take the place of the gods. The prophet calls on what will outlast the people to hear their case.
